items.title: Puerto Vallarta Artists Take Frida Kahlo Tribute to London
items.author: BanderasNews
items.feed_text:
Puerto Vallarta’s artistic community is preparing for an international showcase as a group of local painters and visual artists head to London, England, to participate in 100 Fridas for Frida , a collective exhibition honoring the life, work and legacy of Mexican artist Frida Kahlo.

The local participation is being coordinated by Isela Mariscal of the Real P Network. Six Vallarta artists – Caty Huet, Dinorah Gómez, Javier Niño, Gonzalo Espinosa, Claudia Ríos and Isela Mariscal – will travel to the United Kingdom to attend the exhibition. Rosana Chávez, Mónica Gurrola and Gloria Benavides will also be represented through works they are sending for the event.

The second edition of 100 Fridas for Frida will open September 3, 2026, at Blank Canvas gallery in London’s Fulham district. The exhibition brings together the work of 100 creators from different places, each offering a personal interpretation of Kahlo through different perspectives, techniques and artistic approaches.

The exhibition looks beyond the commercial image that has grown around Kahlo and focuses instead on the woman and artist behind the icon. The participating works explore her life, contradictions, identity and the cultural legacy she left in Mexico and around the world.

The project first premiered in Paris, France, as part of the commemoration of the 115th anniversary of Kahlo’s birth. Since then, it has been presented at cultural venues in different locations, including Mexico City. Its arrival in London marks another step in the project’s effort to encourage an international conversation about one of Mexico’s best-known artists.

For the Puerto Vallarta participants, the exhibition offers more than an opportunity to display individual works. Their presence places local artistic talent in an international setting and highlights the depth and diversity of the city’s creative community.

Mariscal and the participating artists emphasized that bringing Puerto Vallarta artwork to another country also means sharing a piece of the city’s identity, creativity and artistic perspective with a wider audience.

During a press conference ahead of their departure, the artists recognized the support of Laurel Carrillo, Councilor for Culture; Ricardo Josué Martínez Andrade, director of the Vallarta Cultural Institute; and the Puerto Vallarta City Council.

Their support, the artists said, reflects a growing interest in strengthening the local arts community and creating opportunities for Vallarta artists to participate in significant cultural projects beyond Mexico.

With the London exhibition approaching, the group is preparing to represent Puerto Vallarta alongside artists from around the world, adding a local perspective to an international tribute to Frida Kahlo.

items.title: Puerto Vallarta Sees Rise in Romantic Vow Renewals

Puerto Vallarta, Mexico – Over the past few months, I’ve noticed a significant increase in requests for beachfront vow renewal ceremonies. This growing trend highlights a shift in how people travel: visitors are no longer just looking to relax or explore new destinations – they are actively seeking meaningful ways to create lasting memories during their vacations.

Renewing marriage vows is no small occasion. Reaching a new milestone in a relationship is a true accomplishment that deserves a memorable celebration. In a world of constant change and uncertainty, enduring love that evolves and grows stronger is something worth celebrating.

The Pacific Coast: A Timeless Backdrop for Lasting Love 

Puerto Vallarta has long been known as a romantic getaway, but today’s trend goes beyond traditional honeymoons and weddings. More and more couples – from those celebrating early anniversaries to those marking silver or golden milestones – are choosing a Vallarta sunset to reaffirm their commitments.

The appeal of these ceremonies lies in their intimacy and personalization. Free from the logistics and stress often tied to a large wedding, a vow renewal offers a relaxed setting focused entirely on the couple and their closest loved ones, framed by gentle ocean breezes and the warmth of the Pacific coast.

The Rise of Elopements and Couple-Focused Travel 

This trend aligns closely with a major movement in romance tourism: elopements and private couples’ getaways.

• Ideal for Couples Traveling Alone: There is no need to plan a large event or manage guest lists. It serves as an opportunity to set aside dedicated time together during a trip, keeping the focus entirely on each other.

items.title: Puerto Vallarta Advances Amado Nervo Road Connection
items.author: BanderasNews
items.feed_text:
Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, Mexico – A major transportation project linking Puerto Vallarta and Bahía de Banderas is nearing the finish line. Construction of the Amado Nervo Bridge, also known as the Ameca River Bridge, is now 90 percent complete and is expected to open in November 2026.

The project is designed to address one of the region’s most persistent transportation challenges: heavy traffic along Federal Highway 200 and the existing crossings between Jalisco and Nayarit. Nayarit Governor Miguel Ángel Navarro Quintero confirmed that the bridge represents an investment of 900 million pesos.

Once completed, the 800-meter-long bridge will provide four lanes of toll-free traffic. It will measure 24 meters wide and is expected to benefit more than 500,000 people who live, work, study or travel between the two municipalities.

The new crossing is also expected to make a noticeable difference in daily travel. By replacing some of the bottlenecks created by the current two-lane intersections, officials estimate that commuters could save nearly 30 minutes each day.

However, the bridge is just one part of a larger transportation project. Complementary construction on the Puerto Vallarta side is scheduled to continue through June 2027, according to Mayor Luis Munguía, who recently inspected progress along the new Avenida Federación.

As part of the project, Avenida Federación will be renamed Amado Nervo, matching the name of the roadway on the Nayarit side. The route is being developed with a concrete surface, three lanes in each direction, bicycle paths, trees and landscaping.

Munguía said the section extending beyond the University Center of the Coast is expected to be completed before February 2027. The city has already allocated funding for this portion through the Municipal Social Infrastructure Fund, known as FAISMUN.

The next phase will include another vehicular bridge and an additional 1.3 kilometers of roadway. Municipal officials are also negotiating with federal authorities to finish the connection from Avenida México to the intersection at Mojoneras by the middle of 2027.

The completed corridor is expected to give commuters an alternative to some of the busiest sections of Federal Highway 200. It will be especially useful for people who cross the state line every day, including employees, students, business owners and visitors.

For students at the University of Guadalajara who live in Bahía de Banderas, the improved connection could mean a simpler trip to campus. It will also benefit residents of Jalisco who travel to Nayarit for work or school.

With the main bridge approaching completion and additional road improvements planned through 2027, the Amado Nervo project is set to become an important part of the region’s growing transportation network.

items.title: Puerto Vallarta’s Ángelo Covarrubias Wins State Title
items.author: BanderasNews

Puerto Vallarta, Jalisco, Mexico – At only 13 years old, Puerto Vallarta singer Ángelo “Angeloo” Covarrubias has added another major achievement to his growing list of musical accomplishments. Representing Puerto Vallarta and the Western Sierra Coast Region, the young performer won first place in the state finals of Suenan las Juventudes , held in Guadalajara.

Angeloo competed against young performers from across Jalisco, ultimately earning the top spot and a 20,000-peso prize for his performance.

Born and raised in Puerto Vallarta, Angeloo began performing publicly about three years ago. Since then, he has become a familiar face on local stages, regularly taking part in singing competitions and other events. His performances have earned him a strong following among both residents and visitors.

Much of his musical development has come through his own determination. Angeloo taught himself to sing and even learned to speak English while playing PlayStation. He can play the piano, guitar and drums and has recently begun learning the saxophone. His talents also extend to the classroom, where he has received recognition for several academic projects.

His growing list of competition victories includes “So You Think You Can Rise 2024,” “Canta Bahía Canta 2024,” “The Voice Kids Zapopan 2025,” and was named the “Vallarta’s Best Young Artist 2026.” In preparation for “Suenan las Juventudes,” he performed weekly at La Catrina Cantina, using each appearance to strengthen his stage presence and prepare for the state competition.

Angeloo also draws inspiration from Dimash Qudaibergen, the acclaimed Kazakh singer known for his extraordinary vocal range. The Puerto Vallarta teenager has incorporated Dimash’s music into his performances and regularly pays tribute to the artist who has influenced his musical journey.

For the state competition, Angeloo performed a Spanish-language version of “SOS,” offering his own tribute to Dimash. The performance connected his admiration for the singer with his own developing style and gave the audience a glimpse of the young artist’s dedication.

Reaching the state finals was also a team effort. Angeloo received support from the government of Puerto Vallarta, led by architect Luis Munguía, along with guidance from the Puerto Vallarta Youth Directorate under Herova Olmos.

His first-place finish puts a young Puerto Vallarta performer in the spotlight at the state level. More than another trophy, the victory reflects the hours of practice, persistence and love of music that have shaped Angeloo’s journey so far.

As he accepted the recognition in Guadalajara, Angeloo carried more than the pride of representing his hometown. Through his music, he also shared a message of peace and love, showing how a young performer can use his voice to reach audiences far beyond the stages where his journey began.

items.title: Six Ways to Experience Puerto Vallarta During the Rainy Season
items.author: BanderasNews
items.feed_text:
Puerto Vallarta takes on a different character from July through October, when afternoon rains refresh the jungle, strengthen waterfalls, and bring cooler temperatures to the coast. With fewer visitors, this season also offers travelers the chance to explore nature and local traditions at a more relaxed pace.

For experienced visitors, the rainy season is an ideal time to discover some of Puerto Vallarta’s outdoor experiences. From jungle waterfalls and marine adventures to gardens in full bloom and sea turtle releases, these activities offer a memorable look at the destination beyond its beaches.

Chase Waterfalls in Yelapa and Quimixto 

Rainfall transforms the waterfalls south of Puerto Vallarta, making summer an excellent time to explore the trails around Yelapa and Quimixto.

In Yelapa, the waterfall known as Cola de Caballo , or Horsetail, becomes especially impressive after seasonal rains. The hike to the High Waterfall takes about 45 minutes from the town center and includes jungle trails and river crossings. Visitors should start early, wear shoes with good traction, and carry a waterproof bag for phones and other belongings.

Quimixto offers a gentler alternative, with a relatively flat trail leading to a waterfall and natural pools. Travelers can also explore the La Puerta River on horseback, making the experience accessible to families and visitors seeking a more leisurely adventure.

Discover Jalisco’s Raicilla Tradition 

The rainy season is also a good opportunity to explore Puerto Vallarta’s connection to raicilla, an artisanal agave spirit with deep roots in the coastal and mountain communities of Jalisco.

At El Tasting Room in the 5 de Diciembre neighborhood near Camarones Beach, visitors can learn about raicilla alongside other Mexican spirits, including tequila, mezcal, and sotol. Guided tastings introduce guests to the history, production methods, and distinctive flavors of these traditional alcoholic beverages.

Raicilla has been part of Jalisco’s cultural heritage since the late 19th century and received its Denomination of Origin in 2019, further recognizing its regional importance.

Snorkel and Dive at Los Arcos 

Los Arcos de Mismaloya is another standout during the summer months. Protected as a marine park since 1984, the iconic granite formations shelter underwater caves, tunnels, and arches inhabited by a variety of marine life.

Snorkelers and divers may encounter angelfish, octopuses, moray eels, and sea turtles. From May through September, warm Pacific waters can provide favorable conditions for exploring the area.

The lower number of visitors during the green season can also mean smaller groups and a more relaxed experience on the water.

See the Botanical Gardens in Full Bloom 

August and September bring abundant growth to the Vallarta Botanical Garden , where seasonal rainfall helps create ideal conditions for tropical plants.

After a rain shower, the gardens take on a fresh appearance, with water droplets covering orchids and other flowers while moss and foliage become especially lush. The scent of wet earth and tropical plants adds another sensory element to a walk beneath palms, ferns, and dense forest.

Visitors can complete their outing with a Mexican meal at Hacienda de Oro, the garden’s on-site restaurant. Because trails may become slippery after rain, sturdy closed-toe shoes and quick-drying clothing are recommended.

Witness a Sea Turtle Release 

From July through December, sea turtles return to Banderas Bay to nest, with activity reaching its peak between August and November. Olive Ridley, Green, and Hawksbill turtles are among the species that come ashore during the season.

Local conservation efforts give visitors an opportunity to witness the next generation of these marine animals make its way to the Pacific. Resorts such as Marriott Puerto Vallarta Resort & Spa participate in conservation programs that help release tens of thousands of hatchlings each year.

Releases are generally held shortly before sunset, when conditions are safer for the young turtles. Events typically begin with information about the nesting season and conservation efforts before the hatchlings are guided toward the water.

Enjoy Puerto Vallarta at a Slower Pace 

The rainy season offers a different way to experience Puerto Vallarta. Seasonal showers refresh the landscape, waterfalls reach their fullest flow, gardens flourish, and marine and wildlife activities take on a special character.

With fewer tourists and plenty of opportunities to explore nature, the green season can be an ideal time for travelers who want to experience Puerto Vallarta at a more relaxed pace while discovering some of the region’s most memorable outdoor attractions.

Puerto Vallarta’s own Ruben Perez has taken a powerful leap forward in his musical journey by remixing and re-releasing his 2023 hit single, “Marry Me.” This fresh take reimagines the original release through a whole new lens, pairing expressive guitar melodies with a deeply soulful vocal performance that breathe new life into the track.

Rather than treating the phrase as a simple question, Perez frames “Marry Me” as a lifelong commitment, exploring how true love evolves beyond initial spark into a conscious decision made day after day.

The accompanying music video brings that idea to life through different couples, locations and moments, including personal images from Perez’s own wedding. It moves from a first encounter at a train station to dancing barefoot on a beach, sharing a rainy evening in Manhattan, raising a family and watching grandchildren grow. Together, the scenes reflect the quiet moments that can become the most meaningful parts of a lifelong relationship.

“Marry Me” also recognizes that lasting love is not always defined by dramatic gestures. Sometimes it is about staying, growing together, laughing together and waking up beside the person you chose years ago.

In that sense, the title is more than a question. It becomes a promise.

Perez’s connection to music began long before Marry Me . A lifelong music enthusiast and self-described “guitarist at heart,” he first explored his creativity by writing down his thoughts and ideas before discovering music as a deeper form of expression.

For more than a decade, he was an active part of Puerto Vallarta’s music scene, performing everything from pop and rock to reggae, punk and metal. As a member of cover bands, he brought his own style to each performance, entertaining audiences at local restaurants, bars, hotels and festivals.

In 2008, Perez made an important change in his musical career, moving his focus from performing to songwriting and composition. The decision gave him more room to develop his own ideas and explore his creative side.

Although he is no longer a full-time professional musician, Perez has continued to write, sing and play guitar on his compositions. His work combines his experience as a performer with the personal approach he has developed as a songwriter.

The new version of “Marry Me” is another chapter in that ongoing creative journey and offers listeners a chance to discover the work of a Puerto Vallarta artist whose connection to music has remained strong for decades.

Music lovers can now listen to the remixed version of “Marry Me” and experience its newly updated visual story on YouTube.

items.title: Getting Older Comes With Some Unexpected Perks
items.author: BanderasNews
items.feed_text:
Puerto Vallarta, Mexico – Mimi Bomba is beginning to appreciate some of the less obvious advantages of getting older. Sure, there may be a few signs of age creeping into daily life, including a new approach to organization that involves leaving things exactly where they fall. But perhaps the biggest change is simply caring less about appearances and other people’s opinions. 

Have you ever dropped something on the floor and thought, “Well, I guess that lives there now.” I did that a few days ago with a pen. Then I was looking for a pen this morning and remembered where one was. I have decided that it is just my new filing system from now on. Not sure what that’s a sign of – age or laziness. Maybe both. Probably both. Yeah, both.

Speaking of age, on the bright side, there are things that used to matter to me, that no longer do. For example, making sure my makeup was perfect before venturing outside. That one is long gone. Now I don’t even worry that I might scare little children if they see my actual naked face.

My brother once told me, “Sister, when you don’t have on makeup, you look like you just got out of prison.” My sweet and kind sister-in-law was appalled that he said that, but I thought it was hysterically funny! And true.

Another “advantage” of getting older is really not caring about what other people think about me. I heard someone say, “It’s none of my business what you think, and it’s none of your business what I think.” That sounds right to me.

I think that’s the reason I am now able to go out in public without applying warpaint to make myself look like Baby Jane. ¡La vida buena! 

Tu Amiga,
MiMi Bomba, la vieja fea

items.title: Guadalajara to Host Latin America’s 50 Best Restaurants
items.author: BanderasNews
items.feed_text:
Guadalajara will take center stage in the regional culinary world this winter as it hosts Latin America’s 50 Best Restaurants awards on December 1, 2026. The ceremony, sponsored by S.Pellegrino & Acqua Panna, gathers top chefs, restaurateurs, and hospitality leaders from across the continent to unveil the year’s official dining rankings.

This marks the first time the Jalisco state capital will host the event, now in its 14th edition. Mexico has hosted three previous ceremonies – twice in Mexico City (2015 and 2016) and once in Mérida (2022) – highlighting the country’s steady influence on the broader regional food scene.

Guadalajara makes a natural fit for the gathering. Long recognized for cultural exports like mariachi and charrería, the city has built a food culture that balances traditional specialties – such as birria, tortas ahogadas, tejuino , and jericalla – with a fast-growing contemporary restaurant scene. Its location near the UNESCO World Heritage agave fields and historic distilleries of Tequila adds deep agricultural roots to that modern momentum.

State officials see the event as a key validation of local efforts. Michelle Fridman Hirsch, Secretary of Tourism for Jalisco, pointed out that hosting the awards reflects years of hard work by local chefs and producers to create a unique culinary identity. She noted that the event also serves as a stepping stone toward Jalisco’s broader “Year of Gastronomy” initiatives planned for 2027.

Before the main December ceremony, organizers will announce three individual awards: the Champions of Change Award for social leadership in hospitality, the Art of Hospitality Award for outstanding service, and the One To Watch Award for an emerging restaurant on the rise.

Since its launch in 2013, Latin America’s 50 Best Restaurants has helped introduce diners around the world to the region’s diverse culinary traditions and innovative restaurant scene. The annual ranking is determined by the Latin America’s 50 Best Restaurants Academy, made up of 300 restaurant industry leaders from across the region.

With Guadalajara as the host city, the 2026 ceremony will offer an international audience another opportunity to discover the flavors, traditions and culinary talent that make Jalisco an important part of Mexico’s food story.

items.title: Puerto Vallarta Adds Five New Police Patrol Vehicles
items.author: BanderasNews
items.feed_text:
Puerto Vallarta is taking another step toward strengthening its local security forces with a fresh wave of resources for city streets. In a recent official ceremony, Mayor Luis Munguía handed over five brand-new pickup truck patrol vehicles to the Municipal Police Station, alongside essential uniforms and tactical equipment for active officers.

The latest vehicles add to the 35 patrol units provided by the municipal government in June. By expanding the fleet, city officials aim to shorten response times, boost operational presence, and cover more ground during routine daily shifts.

Beyond adding wheels on the ground, the city focused on the day-to-day needs of the force itself. Upgraded gear and new uniforms were distributed to help improve working conditions for officers stationed throughout the city. During the event, Mayor Munguía emphasized that equipping law enforcement with modern tools is a core priority for his team, reiterating his administration’s commitment to supporting the men and women on the front lines.

As one of Mexico’s premier coastal destinations, keeping neighborhoods and public areas safe remains a top economic and civic goal. These newly assigned pickup trucks will immediately join active surveillance routes, reinforcing preventive patrols across different sectors to ensure both residents and visitors feel secure.

items.title: Café de Olla: When Morning Coffee Becomes an Experience
items.author: Heather Gray
items.feed_text:
Puerto Vallarta, Mexico – One of my favorite things about living in Mexico has been discovering that some of the simplest things can carry the most history, flavor, and tradition. Café de olla is a perfect example.

If you see café de olla on a menu while you’re in Mexico, order it. At least once. Even if you’re normally an Americano, latte, or plain-black-coffee person, this is one of those traditional Mexican experiences worth trying.

Café de olla literally means “coffee from the pot.” But this isn’t just regular coffee brewed in a different container. Traditionally, café de olla is prepared in an olla de barro , or clay pot, with ground coffee, cinnamon and piloncillo , an unrefined cane sugar commonly used throughout Mexico. Depending on the region or family recipe, you may also find additions such as cloves, star anise, orange peel or even a little chocolate.

A Cup With a Story 

Like many traditional foods and drinks, the exact origin of café de olla isn’t perfectly documented. One of the most commonly told stories traces it to the Mexican Revolution of the early 1900s.

During the Revolution, women known as soldaderas – often called Adelitas – traveled with revolutionary troops. They weren’t simply standing on the sidelines. They cooked, carried supplies, cared for the wounded and, in some cases, fought alongside the men.

According to the popular story, these women prepared coffee in large clay pots over fires, adding piloncillo and cinnamon to create something warm, sweet and energizing for soldiers enduring long days and cold nights.

Historians point out that it’s difficult to identify one person or moment when café de olla was “invented,” and versions of sweetened coffee existed before the Revolution. But the Revolution is strongly associated with the drink’s history and its spread through Mexican culture.

What began as something practical eventually became something deeply traditional.

Café de olla moved from campfires into homes, markets, fondas and restaurants, becoming a drink associated with family, hospitality and mornings around the table. Recipes evolved along the way, which is why the café de olla you drink in one part of Mexico may taste completely different from the next.

And I think that’s part of its charm.

I like drinking mine out of my fancy cups.

Could I pour it into an ordinary coffee mug and drink it while answering emails or running around the house? Of course.

But sometimes I don’t want coffee to simply be the caffeine I consume while moving on to the next thing.

I want to slow down.

I want the beautiful cup. I want to smell the cinnamon. I want to sit for a few minutes and actually taste what I’m drinking. I want to notice the morning instead of racing through it.

There is something to be said for taking an ordinary part of your day and intentionally making it a little more special. Use the beautiful dishes. Sit somewhere you love. Put your phone down. Notice the steam coming off your coffee. Take the extra five minutes.

Sometimes the smallest details are exactly what turn “having a cup of coffee” into having a memorable experience.

Make Café de Olla at Home 

The best part is that you don’t have to find a restaurant serving it. Café de olla is incredibly easy to make at home, and you don’t absolutely need a clay pot to enjoy it.

For about 4 cups, you’ll need:
4 cups water
4–5 tablespoons ground coffee
1 cinnamon stick
Piloncillo – start with about 1–2 ounces and adjust depending on how sweet you like your coffee
Optional: a small piece of orange peel, 1–2 cloves or a star anise

Bring the water and cinnamon to a simmer. Add the piloncillo and stir until it dissolves. Add the coffee, allow it to come just to a gentle simmer, then remove it from the heat. Cover and let everything steep for about 5–10 minutes.

Strain it into your favorite cup and enjoy.

If you have a traditional food-safe olla de barro, even better. Just be sure that any Mexican pottery used for food or drinks is certified lead-free, since some traditional glazed pottery can contain lead.

And then comes the most important part:

Don’t rush it.

Grab the cup you normally “save” for something special. Sit somewhere beautiful. Smell the cinnamon. Take a sip while it’s still hot. Because maybe the special occasion you’ve been saving those beautiful things for is simply this morning.

Have a Healthy day!
Heather
